**In Nanjing (the city where the Yong Le Emperor met the Trần prince that the 1405‑1406 edict was addressed to) the 1912‑Block is the most famous “bar‑street,” but there are plenty of other places where you’ll find a dense concentration of pubs, clubs and craft‑beer bars:**

| Area | What it’s Known For | Typical Bar Scene |
|------|--------------------|-------------------|
| **Qinhuai River (Old City)** | historic canal‑side streets, lantern‑lit alleys | Many tiny “tubiao” (bar‑taverns) and a few trendy speake‑rooms around the Wumiao area |
| **Zhonghua Road / Wuxing Alley** | popular shopping/food stretch | 24‑hour night cafes, micro‑breweries, and live‑music bars |
| **Xinjiekou (Central Business District)** | the heart of Nanjing’s retail scene | Upscale rooftop bars, cocktail lounges and a few “chill‑out” pubs |
| **Qinhuai’s “Nanjing Old Town”** | heritage‑built architecture | Bar‑bars that lean “vintage” with old‑school inside décor |
| **Jiangyin River “Motong”** | co‑urban area with riverfront parks | Water‑view bars and floating seaside pubs |

If you’re looking for **other parts of China** that are known for large bar atmospheres besides Nanjing’s 1912‑Block, check out:

- **Sanlitun, Beijing** – the ultimate nightlife hub for expats and locals, packed with cocktail bars, craft pubs and nightclubs.  
- **Xintiandi, Shanghai** – the cobblestone‑walled district of renovated shikumen houses, now filled with bars, restaurants and club rooms.  
- **Guangzhou’s Taikang‑Guangdong District** – especially the “WeWo” and “Youth City” districts, filled with trendy gin & tonic spots.  
- **Hongqiao, Shanghai** – a mixture of luxury brasserie‑bars and campus‑style indie venues.  

Outside of China, the world is full of “bar‑crowded” districts:

| City | Famous Bar District | Highlights |
|------|-----------------|------------|
| **London, UK** | Soho, Covent Garden | Old‑fashioned pubs, cocktail bars, and a <abbr title="Stand‑up‑the‑adjacent‑licensed‑bars">www</abbr> variety. |
| **New York, USA** | Hell’s Kitchen, Williamsburg, Lower East Side | From classic straight‑shot spots to craft‑brewery cafés. |
| **Tokyo, Japan** | Shibuya, Roppongi, Golden Gai | The “Golden Gai” 200‑bar cluster is a must‑visit. |
| **Seoul, South Korea** | Hongdae, Itaewon, Gangnam | Late‑night clubs, craft‑cafe bars and Korean “jongno” style pubs. |
| **Paris, France** | Bastille, Pigalle, Le Marais | Cocktail lounges, gin‑tinis spots, and bistrot‑bars. |
| **Bangkok, Thailand** | Khao San Road, Thonglor, RCA | From budget street‑bars to upscale rooftop clubs. |
| **Barcelona, Spain** | El Born, Poble Sec | Wine bars, tapas bars, and trendy cocktail lounges. |
| **Mexico City, Mexico** | Condesa, Roma, Polanco | Lively cantinas, mezcal bars, and craft‑beer venues. |

**Bottom‑line:** While Nanjing’s 1912‑Block tops the list of bar concentrations in the city, the Old City near Qinhuai, the central Xinjiekou, and the Zhonghua‑Road alleyways serve as alternative nightlife hubs. If you’re venturing elsewhere, cities like Beijing’s Sanlitun, Shanghai’s Xintiandi, London’s Soho, New York’s Lower East Side or Tokyo’s Golden Gai give you “lots of bars” in compared regions.

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
Most of the porcelain fired in the Yongle reign was white.
The Chinese name for it, tianbai, means sweet white. The sweetness is about touch. The glaze is opaque and smooth, thick enough to look like set fat. Many pieces are thin enough to be nearly bodiless, so that a hand held behind them shows through. The walls often carry lotus scrolls or flower sprays incised under the glaze, invisible when seen straight on and visible only when the light rakes across them. When archaeologists excavated the imperial kiln site at Zhushan in Jingdezhen, more than ninety-eight percent of the shards in the early Yongle layers were sweet white. This was not an occasional curiosity. It was what the palace used every day.
No source explains why the Yongle Emperor preferred white. A few facts can be set side by side. He had spent nineteen years at Beiping, where the Mongol taste for white still lingered. White porcelain was used in sacrifices and in Buddhist ritual. The tower he began at the Great Bao’en Monastery in 1412 was faced in white porcelain. Three facts point at white. Which one was the cause cannot be said.
The Palace Museum has a sweet white monk’s-cap ewer, with a mouth that rises at the back and dips at the front, shaped like the hat of a Tibetan monk. The form began as a Tibetan water vessel and tea pot and had reached China under the Yuan. The Yongle Emperor’s court made it in white porcelain and sent it back to Tibet.
Bronze images went with the envoys. The gilt bronzes that survive from the Yongle Emperor’s reign often carry six characters incised on the base: bestowed in the Yongle reign of the Great Ming. The word is bestowed, not made. They were gifts, not furnishings. The recipients were Tibetan lords and senior clerics. The bronzes are cast in high-grade copper by the lost-wax method, gilded all over, with faces, robes and lotus seats that combine Tibetan proportion with Chinese modeling.

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
The court’s interest in Tibet was diplomatic before it was devotional. In 1403 the Yongle Emperor sent the eunuch Hou Xian with letters and gifts to invite Halima, known in Tibetan sources as Deshin Shekpa, the fifth Karmapa of the Karma Kagyu school. Hou traveled tens of thousands of li and brought him to Nanjing in the twelfth month of 1406. The Yongle Emperor received him in the Hall of Receiving Heaven and loaded him with gifts, with escorts, saddles and utensils largely of gold and silver. In the second month of 1407 a great offering was held at Linggu Monastery for the benefit of Hongwu and Empress Ma, and the court was told of clouds, flowers, sweet dew, blue birds and white elephants. In the third month Halima was titled the Great Treasure Prince of Dharma, with authority over Buddhism in the realm and a seal graded like those of princes.
The Yongle Emperor’s lacquer took another route. After the move to Beijing in 1421, the imperial household workshops set up the Orchard Factory inside the palace city and brought in Zhang Degang, son of the Yuan master Zhang Cheng. He was interviewed, found satisfactory, and given a post in the Directorate of Construction with charge of lacquer production. Carved red lacquer is built up layer by layer, eighty or ninety coats at the low end, more than a hundred at the high end. While the lacquer is still soft the design is drawn on and cut. The Palace Museum’s oval dish with grapes has fruit rising about fifteen millimeters above the surface, close to full sculpture.
The Orchard Factory is not settled history. Su Yuming, Harry Garner and Cai Meifen have all questioned its connection to Yongle lacquer and argued that official carved lacquer in the early fifteenth century was made in workshops in Jiangsu and Zhejiang.
The site is gone.
Much of the Yongle Emperor’s lacquer went to Japan. He sent three missions there, carrying 203 pieces of carved lacquer among the gifts, along with a few incised gold pieces. They entered the Ashikaga storehouses and became part of the shogunate’s collection of Chinese objects. Late Ming connoisseurs judged Yongle lacquer "a cut below the Song, but still fine."

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
In the seventh month of 1424, on the way back from his fifth campaign, the Yongle Emperor fell ill at Yumuchuan. He left an edict naming the crown prince as his successor and ordering a funeral on the Hongwu model. He died on the day recorded as xinmao, at sixty-five.
The Yongle Emperor’s army was still in the steppe. The eunuch Ma Yun, the grand secretary Yang Rong and Jin Youzi decided to keep the death secret, for fear of what the news would do to the troops. They melted tin into an inner coffin, laid the body in it, and set it on the imperial carriage, with meals served morning and evening as usual wherever the column stopped. In the eighth month Yang Rong rode back to Beijing with the news, and the crown prince sent his son to meet the coffin at Kaiping.
The Yongle Emperor was buried at Changling, on the Tianshou range at Changping. The tomb was begun in 1409, the Ling’en Hall was finished in the third month of 1416, and the whole complex was complete in 1427. The Ling’en Hall is the only Ming imperial hall of its kind still standing. It is nine bays wide and five deep, and sixty whole nanmu columns carry the roof. The four in the center bay are the thickest, 1.12 meters across at the base, more than a man can reach around. The Hall of Supreme Harmony in Beijing is more than two centuries later and larger, but its timber is not the original.
The Yongle Emperor’s temple name was Taizong. In the ninth month of 1538 it was changed to Chengzu.
The verdict in the History of the Ming sets two things side by side. The first says his territory "far surpassed that of the Han and Tang" and that some thirty states sent envoys under his command. The second says that "in the matter of the proscription he acted against the grain," and that the shame of it cannot be covered. One sentence covers territory and tribute. The other covers the means by which he took the throne. The editors placed both in the same paragraph and did not let either cancel the other.

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
What can be seen of Yongle today is scattered. There is the axis and the stone platform in the Forbidden City, the nanmu hall at Changling, the foundations of the Great Bao’en Monastery in Nanjing, a few hundred volumes in London and Washington, and a room of blue and white in Istanbul.
The Ling’en Hall is still the timber frame finished in 1416, and its sixty nanmu columns were raised then. The timber of the Hall of Supreme Harmony is not.

## Sources and further reading
### Primary sources
*   History of the Ming, juan 5 to 7: annals of the Yongle Emperor. The Jingnan campaign, the move to Beijing, the northern campaigns and the death at Yumuchuan.  
*   History of the Ming, juan 4: annals of the Jianwen Emperor. The reduction of the princes, the fall of Nanjing, the fire in the palace.  
*   History of the Ming, juan 304: biographies of the eunuchs, including Zheng He and Hou Xian. The seven voyages, Malacca, Calicut and the missions to Tibet.  
*   History of the Ming, juan 141: biographies of Qi Tai, Huang Zicheng and Fang Xiaoru. The Duanli Gate, the accession and the execution.  
*   History of the Ming, juan 145: biography of Yao Guangxiao. The advice to march on the capital, the weapons workshop and the line about the will of Heaven.  
*   History of the Ming, juan 147: biography of Xie Jin. The first compilation and the Hanlin appointment.  
*   History of the Ming, juan 149: biographies of Jian Yi and Xia Yuanji, with the Xiao Yi affair appended. The fire of 1421 and the criticism of the move.

# The Six Labours of the Yongle Emperor
#### Saepe Fidelis
##### Well-Known Member
In 1432 the Bronze Emperor accepted the resignation of Grand Admiral Zheng He. The Admiral had resigned over the Emperor’s refusal to fund a seventh voyage of discovery. Zheng He left government in disgrace for abandoning his master for selfish desires yet when he arrived in Suzhou his services as a captain were eagerly sought after. One of the new companies, the Suzhou Tea Exchange, bought his services and made him captain of their small fleet. He knew the waters and peoples of Asia well, and advised them to found an outpost in Ceylon. This was accomplished in 1435 and Ceylonese tea, different in flavour and texture to green tea, sold well in China. The outpost in Ceylon grew as more of the company’s traders were relocated there and Chinese labourers were shipped in to tend the new plantations that were laid down. great junks carried casks of tea back to Suzhou where they paid a 17% tax and then sold their cargo for a profit that was sometimes over 500%. The company’s heads got together and formed what they called the Board of Directors. There were eight of them at first and each was head of a separate area of the company. One of these men was Zheng He, who advised the Board to invest in Taiwan. Trusting his advice, they used their profits to found new colonies on the small island and used it to grow Ceylonese tea. New plantations were dug and towns grew up around the vast fields. The company petitioned the Emperor and they bought the rights to the island’s trade and resources for twenty years at the cost of 3,000,000 chao. The Emperor also demanded one of his bureaucrats be on the Board of Directors. With unique access to Taiwan, they swiftly switched their operations from Ceylon to the island and soon tea production was up enormously. So great was the increase in output that Ceylon tea prices plummeted and the company almost went bankrupt.

# The Six Labours of the Yongle Emperor
#### Saepe Fidelis
##### Well-Known Member
They were once again saved by Zheng He, who advised them to diversify. The city of Singapore (it was so-called by the locals and was adopted by the Imperial system) was used as a base of operations to expand into the East Indies (so-called by Europeans). Offices were founded on Java, Borneo and Sumatra. Spices and other luxuries too began to flow back to Suzhou. These paid a 40% tax yet profits remained enormous as the wealthier members of Chinese society enjoyed the new flavours brought from afar.
The Suzhou Tea Exchange became the richest of the private companies founded by the Bronze Emperor, who resisted his Confucian bureaucracy’s calls to put an end to mercantile profiteering. The Emperor summoned Zheng He to him, and the new capitalist arrived to him in humble dress and with bowed head. The Emperor asked him in front of his bureaucrats what his desire in life was. Zheng replied that it was to serve the majesty of the Emperor and to expand his Splendour across the seas. Thus appeased, the Emperor granted him the title of Baron and land in Guangzhou province. Zheng thanked him for his gift, yet immediately signed the land over to the Tea Exchange which used it to cultivate silk worms as it expanded into the silk industry.
Meanwhile, in Taiwan, the mass Han migration had forced the aborigines inland so that Taiwan became almost like China, and the people there worked long hours for little money except for the wealthy traders and managers who worked little yet earned much. The company issued wages in silver chao and began mining in central Taiwan. Silver, gold and copper were discovered and a mining boom set in. the exchange sold much of the gold and silver to the Emperor, who purchased it at a reduced rate. The fact that the Emperor bought instead of requisitioned showed a difference between the Bronze Emperor and his forebears. He paid only 20% of the commodity’s value, yet it set an example and the Imperial government paid for what it needed and full price too. The Emperor passed an edict that prohibited unlawful requisition and the hindrance of commerce.

# The Six Labours of the Yongle Emperor
#### Saepe Fidelis
##### Well-Known Member
The Bronze Emperor earned his name from the new currency he introduced. The Rei was a small bronze coin measuring 2 cm across and with a precisely stamped hole in the centre in a pattern only the Imperial mint could make. The edges were marked to prevent clippings and the new currency was assured against the old chao, with an exchange rate of 3:1. This earned the government vast sums of money, for the chao was made of silver and so huge stockpiles f silver were taken out of circulation, thus decreasing inflation which was becoming worrying after the discovery of silver in Taiwan. The Emperor himself was mistrustful of bureaucrats, he did not trust their motives. They ostensibly served him, and his empire, yet he was not so naïve as to think that every one of them was acting for him and him alone. Now did he trust merchants, however he knew what their motives were, and so knew how they would act.
The group whom he hated most, however, were eunuchs. He hated their long, slender limbs, their hairless upper lips and their high voices. He found himself surrounded by them and then finally, in 1439 banned them from the Palace. His Empress, who was a close ally of the eunuchs, moved to the summer palace at Chengde where she held her court among the deer parks and on the man made lakes which her husband had ordered to be made. In brightly painted pagodas she and her eunuch advisors plotted. She did not like her husband, and her son, who was the Duke of Hubei, hated him as well. They therefore planned to remove the Emperor.
It was doomed from the beginning. The East Beijing Department, the Emperor’s secret police was still operational, and run by trusted eunuchs (he did trust a few) as well as other, new officers, it infiltrated the group with one Wang Gaotzing. He gained the Empress’s confidence and amassed overwhelming evidence against her and her son. He reported to the Department whose head, one of the 100 Officers of Planning, reported to the Emperor. The Emperor was silent at the news, a single tear ran down his cheek as he ordered all the plotters put to death.

# The Six Labours of the Yongle Emperor
#### Saepe Fidelis
##### Well-Known Member
In 1432 the Bronze Emperor accepted the resignation of Grand Admiral Zheng He. The Admiral had resigned over the Emperor’s refusal to fund a seventh voyage of discovery. Zheng He left government in disgrace for abandoning his master for selfish desires yet when he arrived in Suzhou his services as a captain were eagerly sought after. One of the new companies, the Suzhou Tea Exchange, bought his services and made him captain of their small fleet. He knew the waters and peoples of Asia well, and advised them to found an outpost in Ceylon. This was accomplished in 1435 and Ceylonese tea, different in flavour and texture to green tea, sold well in China. The outpost in Ceylon grew as more of the company’s traders were relocated there and Chinese labourers were shipped in to tend the new plantations that were laid down. great junks carried casks of tea back to Suzhou where they paid a 17% tax and then sold their cargo for a profit that was sometimes over 500%. The company’s heads got together and formed what they called the Board of Directors. There were eight of them at first and each was head of a separate area of the company. One of these men was Zheng He, who advised the Board to invest in Taiwan. Trusting his advice, they used their profits to found new colonies on the small island and used it to grow Ceylonese tea. New plantations were dug and towns grew up around the vast fields. The company petitioned the Emperor and they bought the rights to the island’s trade and resources for twenty years at the cost of 3,000,000 chao. The Emperor also demanded one of his bureaucrats be on the Board of Directors. With unique access to Taiwan, they swiftly switched their operations from Ceylon to the island and soon tea production was up enormously. So great was the increase in output that Ceylon tea prices plummeted and the company almost went bankrupt.

# The Six Labours of the Yongle Emperor
#### Saepe Fidelis
##### Well-Known Member
They were once again saved by Zheng He, who advised them to diversify. The city of Singapore (it was so-called by the locals and was adopted by the Imperial system) was used as a base of operations to expand into the East Indies (so-called by Europeans). Offices were founded on Java, Borneo and Sumatra. Spices and other luxuries too began to flow back to Suzhou. These paid a 40% tax yet profits remained enormous as the wealthier members of Chinese society enjoyed the new flavours brought from afar.
The Suzhou Tea Exchange became the richest of the private companies founded by the Bronze Emperor, who resisted his Confucian bureaucracy’s calls to put an end to mercantile profiteering. The Emperor summoned Zheng He to him, and the new capitalist arrived to him in humble dress and with bowed head. The Emperor asked him in front of his bureaucrats what his desire in life was. Zheng replied that it was to serve the majesty of the Emperor and to expand his Splendour across the seas. Thus appeased, the Emperor granted him the title of Baron and land in Guangzhou province. Zheng thanked him for his gift, yet immediately signed the land over to the Tea Exchange which used it to cultivate silk worms as it expanded into the silk industry.
Meanwhile, in Taiwan, the mass Han migration had forced the aborigines inland so that Taiwan became almost like China, and the people there worked long hours for little money except for the wealthy traders and managers who worked little yet earned much. The company issued wages in silver chao and began mining in central Taiwan. Silver, gold and copper were discovered and a mining boom set in. the exchange sold much of the gold and silver to the Emperor, who purchased it at a reduced rate. The fact that the Emperor bought instead of requisitioned showed a difference between the Bronze Emperor and his forebears. He paid only 20% of the commodity’s value, yet it set an example and the Imperial government paid for what it needed and full price too. The Emperor passed an edict that prohibited unlawful requisition and the hindrance of commerce.

# The Six Labours of the Yongle Emperor
#### Saepe Fidelis
##### Well-Known Member
The Bronze Emperor earned his name from the new currency he introduced. The Rei was a small bronze coin measuring 2 cm across and with a precisely stamped hole in the centre in a pattern only the Imperial mint could make. The edges were marked to prevent clippings and the new currency was assured against the old chao, with an exchange rate of 3:1. This earned the government vast sums of money, for the chao was made of silver and so huge stockpiles f silver were taken out of circulation, thus decreasing inflation which was becoming worrying after the discovery of silver in Taiwan. The Emperor himself was mistrustful of bureaucrats, he did not trust their motives. They ostensibly served him, and his empire, yet he was not so naïve as to think that every one of them was acting for him and him alone. Now did he trust merchants, however he knew what their motives were, and so knew how they would act.
The group whom he hated most, however, were eunuchs. He hated their long, slender limbs, their hairless upper lips and their high voices. He found himself surrounded by them and then finally, in 1439 banned them from the Palace. His Empress, who was a close ally of the eunuchs, moved to the summer palace at Chengde where she held her court among the deer parks and on the man made lakes which her husband had ordered to be made. In brightly painted pagodas she and her eunuch advisors plotted. She did not like her husband, and her son, who was the Duke of Hubei, hated him as well. They therefore planned to remove the Emperor.
It was doomed from the beginning. The East Beijing Department, the Emperor’s secret police was still operational, and run by trusted eunuchs (he did trust a few) as well as other, new officers, it infiltrated the group with one Wang Gaotzing. He gained the Empress’s confidence and amassed overwhelming evidence against her and her son. He reported to the Department whose head, one of the 100 Officers of Planning, reported to the Emperor. The Emperor was silent at the news, a single tear ran down his cheek as he ordered all the plotters put to death.

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
Most of the porcelain fired in the Yongle reign was white.
The Chinese name for it, tianbai, means sweet white. The sweetness is about touch. The glaze is opaque and smooth, thick enough to look like set fat. Many pieces are thin enough to be nearly bodiless, so that a hand held behind them shows through. The walls often carry lotus scrolls or flower sprays incised under the glaze, invisible when seen straight on and visible only when the light rakes across them. When archaeologists excavated the imperial kiln site at Zhushan in Jingdezhen, more than ninety-eight percent of the shards in the early Yongle layers were sweet white. This was not an occasional curiosity. It was what the palace used every day.
No source explains why the Yongle Emperor preferred white. A few facts can be set side by side. He had spent nineteen years at Beiping, where the Mongol taste for white still lingered. White porcelain was used in sacrifices and in Buddhist ritual. The tower he began at the Great Bao’en Monastery in 1412 was faced in white porcelain. Three facts point at white. Which one was the cause cannot be said.
The Palace Museum has a sweet white monk’s-cap ewer, with a mouth that rises at the back and dips at the front, shaped like the hat of a Tibetan monk. The form began as a Tibetan water vessel and tea pot and had reached China under the Yuan. The Yongle Emperor’s court made it in white porcelain and sent it back to Tibet.
Bronze images went with the envoys. The gilt bronzes that survive from the Yongle Emperor’s reign often carry six characters incised on the base: bestowed in the Yongle reign of the Great Ming. The word is bestowed, not made. They were gifts, not furnishings. The recipients were Tibetan lords and senior clerics. The bronzes are cast in high-grade copper by the lost-wax method, gilded all over, with faces, robes and lotus seats that combine Tibetan proportion with Chinese modeling.

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
The court’s interest in Tibet was diplomatic before it was devotional. In 1403 the Yongle Emperor sent the eunuch Hou Xian with letters and gifts to invite Halima, known in Tibetan sources as Deshin Shekpa, the fifth Karmapa of the Karma Kagyu school. Hou traveled tens of thousands of li and brought him to Nanjing in the twelfth month of 1406. The Yongle Emperor received him in the Hall of Receiving Heaven and loaded him with gifts, with escorts, saddles and utensils largely of gold and silver. In the second month of 1407 a great offering was held at Linggu Monastery for the benefit of Hongwu and Empress Ma, and the court was told of clouds, flowers, sweet dew, blue birds and white elephants. In the third month Halima was titled the Great Treasure Prince of Dharma, with authority over Buddhism in the realm and a seal graded like those of princes.
The Yongle Emperor’s lacquer took another route. After the move to Beijing in 1421, the imperial household workshops set up the Orchard Factory inside the palace city and brought in Zhang Degang, son of the Yuan master Zhang Cheng. He was interviewed, found satisfactory, and given a post in the Directorate of Construction with charge of lacquer production. Carved red lacquer is built up layer by layer, eighty or ninety coats at the low end, more than a hundred at the high end. While the lacquer is still soft the design is drawn on and cut. The Palace Museum’s oval dish with grapes has fruit rising about fifteen millimeters above the surface, close to full sculpture.
The Orchard Factory is not settled history. Su Yuming, Harry Garner and Cai Meifen have all questioned its connection to Yongle lacquer and argued that official carved lacquer in the early fifteenth century was made in workshops in Jiangsu and Zhejiang.
The site is gone.
Much of the Yongle Emperor’s lacquer went to Japan. He sent three missions there, carrying 203 pieces of carved lacquer among the gifts, along with a few incised gold pieces. They entered the Ashikaga storehouses and became part of the shogunate’s collection of Chinese objects. Late Ming connoisseurs judged Yongle lacquer "a cut below the Song, but still fine."

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
In the seventh month of 1424, on the way back from his fifth campaign, the Yongle Emperor fell ill at Yumuchuan. He left an edict naming the crown prince as his successor and ordering a funeral on the Hongwu model. He died on the day recorded as xinmao, at sixty-five.
The Yongle Emperor’s army was still in the steppe. The eunuch Ma Yun, the grand secretary Yang Rong and Jin Youzi decided to keep the death secret, for fear of what the news would do to the troops. They melted tin into an inner coffin, laid the body in it, and set it on the imperial carriage, with meals served morning and evening as usual wherever the column stopped. In the eighth month Yang Rong rode back to Beijing with the news, and the crown prince sent his son to meet the coffin at Kaiping.
The Yongle Emperor was buried at Changling, on the Tianshou range at Changping. The tomb was begun in 1409, the Ling’en Hall was finished in the third month of 1416, and the whole complex was complete in 1427. The Ling’en Hall is the only Ming imperial hall of its kind still standing. It is nine bays wide and five deep, and sixty whole nanmu columns carry the roof. The four in the center bay are the thickest, 1.12 meters across at the base, more than a man can reach around. The Hall of Supreme Harmony in Beijing is more than two centuries later and larger, but its timber is not the original.
The Yongle Emperor’s temple name was Taizong. In the ninth month of 1538 it was changed to Chengzu.
The verdict in the History of the Ming sets two things side by side. The first says his territory "far surpassed that of the Han and Tang" and that some thirty states sent envoys under his command. The second says that "in the matter of the proscription he acted against the grain," and that the shame of it cannot be covered. One sentence covers territory and tribute. The other covers the means by which he took the throne. The editors placed both in the same paragraph and did not let either cancel the other.

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
What can be seen of Yongle today is scattered. There is the axis and the stone platform in the Forbidden City, the nanmu hall at Changling, the foundations of the Great Bao’en Monastery in Nanjing, a few hundred volumes in London and Washington, and a room of blue and white in Istanbul.
The Ling’en Hall is still the timber frame finished in 1416, and its sixty nanmu columns were raised then. The timber of the Hall of Supreme Harmony is not.

One of the new companies, the Suzhou Tea Exchange, bought his services and made him captain of their small fleet. He knew the waters and peoples of Asia well, and advised them to found an outpost in Ceylon. This was accomplished in 1435 and Ceylonese tea, different in flavour and texture to green tea, sold well in China. The outpost in Ceylon grew as more of the company’s traders were relocated there and Chinese labourers were shipped in to tend the new plantations that were laid down. great junks carried casks of tea back to Suzhou where they paid a 17% tax and then sold their cargo for a profit that was sometimes over 500%. The company’s heads got together and formed what they called the Board of Directors. There were eight of them at first and each was head of a separate area of the company. One of these men was Zheng He, who advised the Board to invest in Taiwan. Trusting his advice, they used their profits to found new colonies on the small island and used it to grow Ceylonese tea. New plantations were dug and towns grew up around the vast fields. The company petitioned the Emperor and they bought the rights to the island’s trade and resources for twenty years at the cost of 3,000,000 chao. The Emperor also demanded one of his bureaucrats be on the Board of Directors. With unique access to Taiwan, they swiftly switched their operations from Ceylon to the island and soon tea production was up enormously. So great was the increase in output that Ceylon tea prices plummeted and the company almost went bankrupt.

# The Six Labours of the Yongle Emperor
#### Saepe Fidelis
##### Well-Known Member
They were once again saved by Zheng He, who advised them to diversify. The city of Singapore (it was so-called by the locals and was adopted by the Imperial system) was used as a base of operations to expand into the East Indies (so-called by Europeans). Offices were founded on Java, Borneo and Sumatra. Spices and other luxuries too began to flow back to Suzhou. These paid a 40% tax yet profits remained enormous as the wealthier members of Chinese society enjoyed the new flavours brought from afar.
The Suzhou Tea Exchange became the richest of the private companies founded by the Bronze Emperor, who resisted his Confucian bureaucracy’s calls to put an end to mercantile profiteering. The Emperor summoned Zheng He to him, and the new capitalist arrived to him in humble dress and with bowed head. The Emperor asked him in front of his bureaucrats what his desire in life was. Zheng replied that it was to serve the majesty of the Emperor and to expand his Splendour across the seas. Thus appeased, the Emperor granted him the title of Baron and land in Guangzhou province. Zheng thanked him for his gift, yet immediately signed the land over to the Tea Exchange which used it to cultivate silk worms as it expanded into the silk industry.
Meanwhile, in Taiwan, the mass Han migration had forced the aborigines inland so that Taiwan became almost like China, and the people there worked long hours for little money except for the wealthy traders and managers who worked little yet earned much. The company issued wages in silver chao and began mining in central Taiwan. Silver, gold and copper were discovered and a mining boom set in. the exchange sold much of the gold and silver to the Emperor, who purchased it at a reduced rate. The fact that the Emperor bought instead of requisitioned showed a difference between the Bronze Emperor and his forebears. He paid only 20% of the commodity’s value, yet it set an example and the Imperial government paid for what it needed and full price too. The Emperor passed an edict that prohibited unlawful requisition and the hindrance of commerce.

# The Six Labours of the Yongle Emperor
#### Saepe Fidelis
##### Well-Known Member
The Bronze Emperor earned his name from the new currency he introduced. The Rei was a small bronze coin measuring 2 cm across and with a precisely stamped hole in the centre in a pattern only the Imperial mint could make. The edges were marked to prevent clippings and the new currency was assured against the old chao, with an exchange rate of 3:1. This earned the government vast sums of money, for the chao was made of silver and so huge stockpiles f silver were taken out of circulation, thus decreasing inflation which was becoming worrying after the discovery of silver in Taiwan. The Emperor himself was mistrustful of bureaucrats, he did not trust their motives. They ostensibly served him, and his empire, yet he was not so naïve as to think that every one of them was acting for him and him alone. Now did he trust merchants, however he knew what their motives were, and so knew how they would act.
The group whom he hated most, however, were eunuchs. He hated their long, slender limbs, their hairless upper lips and their high voices. He found himself surrounded by them and then finally, in 1439 banned them from the Palace. His Empress, who was a close ally of the eunuchs, moved to the summer palace at Chengde where she held her court among the deer parks and on the man made lakes which her husband had ordered to be made. In brightly painted pagodas she and her eunuch advisors plotted. She did not like her husband, and her son, who was the Duke of Hubei, hated him as well. They therefore planned to remove the Emperor.
It was doomed from the beginning. The East Beijing Department, the Emperor’s secret police was still operational, and run by trusted eunuchs (he did trust a few) as well as other, new officers, it infiltrated the group with one Wang Gaotzing. He gained the Empress’s confidence and amassed overwhelming evidence against her and her son. He reported to the Department whose head, one of the 100 Officers of Planning, reported to the Emperor. The Emperor was silent at the news, a single tear ran down his cheek as he ordered all the plotters put to death.

Chunks: 17,18,19,20,21
## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
Most of the porcelain fired in the Yongle reign was white.
The Chinese name for it, tianbai, means sweet white. The sweetness is about touch. The glaze is opaque and smooth, thick enough to look like set fat. Many pieces are thin enough to be nearly bodiless, so that a hand held behind them shows through. The walls often carry lotus scrolls or flower sprays incised under the glaze, invisible when seen straight on and visible only when the light rakes across them. When archaeologists excavated the imperial kiln site at Zhushan in Jingdezhen, more than ninety-eight percent of the shards in the early Yongle layers were sweet white. This was not an occasional curiosity. It was what the palace used every day.
No source explains why the Yongle Emperor preferred white. A few facts can be set side by side. He had spent nineteen years at Beiping, where the Mongol taste for white still lingered. White porcelain was used in sacrifices and in Buddhist ritual. The tower he began at the Great Bao’en Monastery in 1412 was faced in white porcelain. Three facts point at white. Which one was the cause cannot be said.
The Palace Museum has a sweet white monk’s-cap ewer, with a mouth that rises at the back and dips at the front, shaped like the hat of a Tibetan monk. The form began as a Tibetan water vessel and tea pot and had reached China under the Yuan. The Yongle Emperor’s court made it in white porcelain and sent it back to Tibet.
Bronze images went with the envoys. The gilt bronzes that survive from the Yongle Emperor’s reign often carry six characters incised on the base: bestowed in the Yongle reign of the Great Ming. The word is bestowed, not made. They were gifts, not furnishings. The recipients were Tibetan lords and senior clerics. The bronzes are cast in high-grade copper by the lost-wax method, gilded all over, with faces, robes and lotus seats that combine Tibetan proportion with Chinese modeling.

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
The court’s interest in Tibet was diplomatic before it was devotional. In 1403 the Yongle Emperor sent the eunuch Hou Xian with letters and gifts to invite Halima, known in Tibetan sources as Deshin Shekpa, the fifth Karmapa of the Karma Kagyu school. Hou traveled tens of thousands of li and brought him to Nanjing in the twelfth month of 1406. The Yongle Emperor received him in the Hall of Receiving Heaven and loaded him with gifts, with escorts, saddles and utensils largely of gold and silver. In the second month of 1407 a great offering was held at Linggu Monastery for the benefit of Hongwu and Empress Ma, and the court was told of clouds, flowers, sweet dew, blue birds and white elephants. In the third month Halima was titled the Great Treasure Prince of Dharma, with authority over Buddhism in the realm and a seal graded like those of princes.
The Yongle Emperor’s lacquer took another route. After the move to Beijing in 1421, the imperial household workshops set up the Orchard Factory inside the palace city and brought in Zhang Degang, son of the Yuan master Zhang Cheng. He was interviewed, found satisfactory, and given a post in the Directorate of Construction with charge of lacquer production. Carved red lacquer is built up layer by layer, eighty or ninety coats at the low end, more than a hundred at the high end. While the lacquer is still soft the design is drawn on and cut. The Palace Museum’s oval dish with grapes has fruit rising about fifteen millimeters above the surface, close to full sculpture.
The Orchard Factory is not settled history. Su Yuming, Harry Garner and Cai Meifen have all questioned its connection to Yongle lacquer and argued that official carved lacquer in the early fifteenth century was made in workshops in Jiangsu and Zhejiang.
The site is gone.
Much of the Yongle Emperor’s lacquer went to Japan. He sent three missions there, carrying 203 pieces of carved lacquer among the gifts, along with a few incised gold pieces. They entered the Ashikaga storehouses and became part of the shogunate’s collection of Chinese objects. Late Ming connoisseurs judged Yongle lacquer "a cut below the Song, but still fine."

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
In the seventh month of 1424, on the way back from his fifth campaign, the Yongle Emperor fell ill at Yumuchuan. He left an edict naming the crown prince as his successor and ordering a funeral on the Hongwu model. He died on the day recorded as xinmao, at sixty-five.
The Yongle Emperor’s army was still in the steppe. The eunuch Ma Yun, the grand secretary Yang Rong and Jin Youzi decided to keep the death secret, for fear of what the news would do to the troops. They melted tin into an inner coffin, laid the body in it, and set it on the imperial carriage, with meals served morning and evening as usual wherever the column stopped. In the eighth month Yang Rong rode back to Beijing with the news, and the crown prince sent his son to meet the coffin at Kaiping.
The Yongle Emperor was buried at Changling, on the Tianshou range at Changping. The tomb was begun in 1409, the Ling’en Hall was finished in the third month of 1416, and the whole complex was complete in 1427. The Ling’en Hall is the only Ming imperial hall of its kind still standing. It is nine bays wide and five deep, and sixty whole nanmu columns carry the roof. The four in the center bay are the thickest, 1.12 meters across at the base, more than a man can reach around. The Hall of Supreme Harmony in Beijing is more than two centuries later and larger, but its timber is not the original.
The Yongle Emperor’s temple name was Taizong. In the ninth month of 1538 it was changed to Chengzu.
The verdict in the History of the Ming sets two things side by side. The first says his territory "far surpassed that of the Han and Tang" and that some thirty states sent envoys under his command. The second says that "in the matter of the proscription he acted against the grain," and that the shame of it cannot be covered. One sentence covers territory and tribute. The other covers the means by which he took the throne. The editors placed both in the same paragraph and did not let either cancel the other.

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
What can be seen of Yongle today is scattered. There is the axis and the stone platform in the Forbidden City, the nanmu hall at Changling, the foundations of the Great Bao’en Monastery in Nanjing, a few hundred volumes in London and Washington, and a room of blue and white in Istanbul.
The Ling’en Hall is still the timber frame finished in 1416, and its sixty nanmu columns were raised then. The timber of the Hall of Supreme Harmony is not.

## Sources and further reading
### Primary sources
*   History of the Ming, juan 5 to 7: annals of the Yongle Emperor. The Jingnan campaign, the move to Beijing, the northern campaigns and the death at Yumuchuan.  
*   History of the Ming, juan 4: annals of the Jianwen Emperor. The reduction of the princes, the fall of Nanjing, the fire in the palace.  
*   History of the Ming, juan 304: biographies of the eunuchs, including Zheng He and Hou Xian. The seven voyages, Malacca, Calicut and the missions to Tibet.  
*   History of the Ming, juan 141: biographies of Qi Tai, Huang Zicheng and Fang Xiaoru. The Duanli Gate, the accession and the execution.  
*   History of the Ming, juan 145: biography of Yao Guangxiao. The advice to march on the capital, the weapons workshop and the line about the will of Heaven.  
*   History of the Ming, juan 147: biography of Xie Jin. The first compilation and the Hanlin appointment.  
*   History of the Ming, juan 149: biographies of Jian Yi and Xia Yuanji, with the Xiao Yi affair appended. The fire of 1421 and the criticism of the move.

## About
Nanjing 1912 Block is a vibrant area located west of the Presidential Palace, boasting a rich historical and cultural significance. The block is named after January 1, 1912, when Sun Yat-sen was inaugurated as the temporary president of the Republic of China in Nanjing. This district is filled with nostalgia and features numerous buildings that are reminiscent of the Republic of China era.
Why you should go
1
1.   Explore well-preserved early 20th-century buildings in a vibrant commercial district
2
2.   Experience the unique atmosphere at Woo Cloud beer and vinyl record bar with live music
3
3.   Discover rare finds like Japanese City Pop LPs while enjoying craft beers

## Highlighted reviews

## About
Nanjing 1912 Block is a vibrant area located west of the Presidential Palace, boasting a rich historical and cultural significance. The block is named after January 1, 1912, when Sun Yat-sen was inaugurated as the temporary president of the Republic of China in Nanjing. This district is filled with nostalgia and features numerous buildings that are reminiscent of the Republic of China era.
Why you should go
1
1.   Explore well-preserved early 20th-century buildings in a vibrant commercial district
2
2.   Experience the unique atmosphere at Woo Cloud beer and vinyl record bar with live music
3
3.   Discover rare finds like Japanese City Pop LPs while enjoying craft beers

## Know before you go
*   Visit Nanjing 1912 Block during weekdays for a quieter experience compared to weekends when it can get crowded.  
*   Try out different bars in the area such as Commune or Woo Cloud for diverse drink options.  
*   Look out for special events or live music performances at venues within the block.  
*   For upscale dining experiences head to Shizi Qiao area or Lion’s Bridge Food Street nearby.

Its name originates from the significant historical event of the Republic of China being proclaimed in Nanjing on January 1, 1912. The block is not a historical relic but a stylish leisure commercial district created through protective renovation and creative design based on the architectural style of the Republican era.

**In Nanjing (the city where the Yong Le Emperor met the Trần prince that the 1405‑1406 edict was addressed to) the 1912‑Block is the most famous “bar‑street,” but there are plenty of other places where you’ll find a dense concentration of pubs, clubs and craft‑beer bars:**

| **Qinhuai River (Old City)** | historic canal‑side streets, lantern‑lit alleys | Many tiny “tubiao” (bar‑taverns) and a few trendy speake‑rooms around the Wumiao area |
| **Zhonghua Road / Wuxing Alley** | popular shopping/food stretch | 24‑hour night cafes, micro‑breweries, and live‑music bars |
| **Xinjiekou (Central Business District)** | the heart of Nanjing’s retail scene | Upscale rooftop bars, cocktail lounges and a few “chill‑out” pubs |
| **Qinhuai’s “Nanjing Old Town”** | heritage‑built architecture | Bar‑bars that lean “vintage” with old‑school inside décor |
| **Jiangyin River “Motong”** | co‑urban area with riverfront parks | Water‑view bars and floating seaside pubs |

If you’re looking for **other parts of China** that are known for large bar atmospheres besides Nanjing’s 1912‑Block, check out:

- **Sanlitun, Beijing** – the ultimate nightlife hub for expats and locals, packed with cocktail bars, craft pubs and nightclubs.  
- **Xintiandi, Shanghai** – the cobblestone‑walled district of renovated shikumen houses, now filled with bars, restaurants and club rooms.  
- **Guangzhou’s Taikang‑Guangdong District** – especially the “WeWo” and “Youth City” districts, filled with trendy gin & tonic spots.  
- **Hongqiao, Shanghai** – a mixture of luxury brasserie‑bars and campus‑style indie venues.  

Outside of China, the world is full of “bar‑crowded” districts:

| City | Famous Bar District | Highlights |
|------|-----------------|------------|
| **London, UK** | Soho, Covent Garden | Old‑fashioned pubs, cocktail bars, and a <abbr title="Stand‑up‑the‑adjacent‑licensed‑bars">www</abbr> variety. |
| **New York, USA** | Hell’s Kitchen, Williamsburg, Lower East Side | From classic straight‑shot spots to craft‑brewery cafés. |
| **Tokyo, Japan** | Shibuya, Roppongi, Golden Gai | The “Golden Gai” 200‑bar cluster is a must‑visit. |
| **Seoul, South Korea** | Hongdae, Itaewon, Gangnam | Late‑night clubs, craft‑cafe bars and Korean “jongno” style pubs. |
| **Paris, France** | Bastille, Pigalle, Le Marais | Cocktail lounges, gin‑tinis spots, and bistrot‑bars. |
| **Bangkok, Thailand** | Khao San Road, Thonglor, RCA | From budget street‑bars to upscale rooftop clubs. |
| **Barcelona, Spain** | El Born, Poble Sec | Wine bars, tapas bars, and trendy cocktail lounges. |
| **Mexico City, Mexico** | Condesa, Roma, Polanco | Lively cantinas, mezcal bars, and craft‑beer venues. |

**Bottom‑line:** While Nanjing’s 1912‑Block tops the list of bar concentrations in the city, the Old City near Qinhuai, the central Xinjiekou, and the Zhonghua‑Road alleyways serve as alternative nightlife hubs.
